claim: Crowding occurs when the presence of nearby features causes highly visible objects to become unrecognizable.
source: Crowding occurs when the presence of nearby features causes highly visible objects to become unrecognizable.
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by established scientific consensus in the crowding literature.

claim: Most available studies show that stereoscopic disparity reduces crowding.
source: Most available studies show that stereoscopic disparity reduces crowding, indicating that crowding may be relatively unimportant in three-dimensional environments.
evidence: This claim summarizes findings from previous research literature.

claim: Most previous studies tested only small stereoscopic differences in depth in which disparity, defocus blur, and accommodation are inconsistent with the real world.
source: However, most previous studies tested only small stereoscopic differences in depth in which disparity, defocus blur, and accommodation are inconsistent with the real world.
evidence: This is a critical evaluation of previous research methods based on review of the literature.

claim: This study investigated how large (0.54–2.25 diopters), real differences in target-flanker depth affect crowding.
source: Using a novel multi-depth plane display, this study investigated how large (0.54–2.25 diopters), real differences in target-flanker depth, representative of those experienced between many objects in the real world, affect crowding.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and parameters of the current study.

claim: Large differences in target-flanker depth increased crowding in the majority of observers.
source: Our findings show that large differences in target-flanker depth increased crowding in the majority of observers, contrary to previous work showing reduced crowding in the presence of small depth differences.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The finding that large differences in target-flanker depth increased crowding is contrary to previous work showing reduced crowding in the presence of small depth differences.
source: Our findings show that large differences in target-flanker depth increased crowding in the majority of observers, contrary to previous work showing reduced crowding in the presence of small depth differences.
evidence: This compares the current findings with previous research literature.

claim: When the target was at fixation depth, crowding was generally more pronounced when the flankers were behind the target as opposed to in front of it.
source: Furthermore, when the target was at fixation depth, crowding was generally more pronounced when the flankers were behind the target as opposed to in front of it.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: When the flankers were at fixation depth, crowding was generally more pronounced when the target was behind the flankers.
source: However, when the flankers were at fixation depth, crowding was generally more pronounced when the target was behind the flankers.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: Crowding from clutter outside the limits of binocular fusion can still have a significant impact on object recognition and visual perception in the peripheral field.
source: These findings suggest that crowding from clutter outside the limits of binocular fusion can still have a significant impact on object recognition and visual perception in the peripheral field.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Crowding has implications for many everyday tasks including driving, reading, and face recognition.
source: Consequently, it is assumed that crowding has a large impact on our daily lives with implications for many everyday visual tasks including driving (Xia et al., 2020), reading (Legge, 2007), and face recognition (Kalpadakis-Smith et al., 2018; Louie et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Crowding has important clinical implications for people with glaucoma.
source: Crowding also has important clinical implications for people with glaucoma (Ogata et al., 2019; Shamsi et al., 2022), as well as for other disorders including central vision impairment (e.g. macular degeneration), amblyopia and dyslexia (Whitney and Levi, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Kooi et al., 1994 were the first to investigate how depth influences crowding.
source: Kooi et al., 1994 were the first to investigate how depth influences crowding.
evidence: This is a historical claim about the research literature supported by citation.

claim: Kooi et al., 1994 found that compared to when a peripheral target and flankers were at the same depth, there was a release from crowding when the target and flankers were stereoscopically presented in crossed (front) and uncrossed (behind) disparities.
source: The authors found that compared to when a peripheral target and flankers were at the same depth, there was a release from crowding when the target and flankers were stereoscopically presented in crossed (front) and uncrossed (behind) disparities (Kooi et al., 1994).
evidence: This summarizes findings from a cited study.

claim: Sayim et al., 2008 found that when flankers were at fixation depth, there was less foveal crowding when the target was stereoscopically presented in front or behind the flankers.
source: Sayim et al., 2008 found that when flankers were at fixation depth, there was less foveal crowding when the target was stereoscopically presented in front or behind the flankers.
evidence: This summarizes findings from a cited study.

claim: Felisberti et al., 2005 found an effect of depth on crowding in the parafovea, but to a more limited extent.
source: Felisberti et al., 2005 also found an effect of depth on crowding in the parafovea, but to a more limited extent.
evidence: This summarizes findings from a cited study.

claim: Felisberti et al., 2005 reported a release from crowding in two out of three subjects when the target appeared behind the flankers, but only in one of the three subjects when the target was in front of the flankers.
source: They reported a release from crowding in two out of three subjects when the target appeared behind the flankers, but only in one of the three subjects when the target was in front of the flankers (Felisberti et al., 2005).
evidence: This summarizes specific findings from a cited study.

claim: Astle et al., 2014 tested the effect of depth on crowding over a range of stereoscopically produced target-flanker disparities (±800 arcsec).
source: Astle et al., 2014 extended on previous research by testing the effect of depth on crowding over a range of stereoscopically produced target-flanker disparities (±800 arcsec).
evidence: This describes the methods of a cited study.

claim: Astle et al., 2014 found that when the target was at fixation depth, increasing target-flanker disparity systematically reduced crowding.
source: In line with previous studies, Astle et al., 2014 found that when the target was at fixation depth, increasing target-flanker disparity systematically reduced crowding.
evidence: This summarizes findings from a cited study.

claim: Astle et al., 2014 found that the release from crowding was asymmetric whereby crowding was greater when the flankers were in front of the target compared to behind it.
source: They also found that the release from crowding was asymmetric whereby crowding was greater when the flankers were in front of the target compared to behind it (Astle et al., 2014).
evidence: This summarizes findings from a cited study.

claim: All previous studies on depth and crowding tested only small depth differences between target and flankers that do not reflect the often-large differences in depth between objects in the real world.
source: However, all the above studies tested only small depth differences between target and flankers that do not reflect the often-large differences in depth between objects in the real world.
evidence: This is a critical evaluation of previous research based on review of the literature.

claim: The generalizability of previous stereoscopic studies to real world depth is limited by the fact that disparity information often does not match with accommodation or defocus blur.
source: Furthermore, the generalizability of these studies to real world depth is also limited by the fact that depth cues were generated stereoscopically. One potential problem with stereo displays is that disparity information often does not match with accommodation or defocus blur which can detrimentally affect depth perception (Hoffman et al., 2008; Watt et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a critical evaluation supported by citations to research on stereo displays.

claim: Four studies have investigated the effect of depth on crowding using a real depth display.
source: To our knowledge, four studies have investigated the effect of depth on crowding using a real depth display.
evidence: This is a summary of the literature based on the authors' review.

claim: All four studies using real depth displays used two orthogonally positioned screens viewed through a half-transparent mirror.
source: All four studies used two orthogonally positioned screens viewed through a half-transparent mirror allowing stimuli to be displayed on two different depth planes simultaneously (Eberhardt et al., 2021; Eberhardt and Huckauf, 2019; Eberhardt and Huckauf, 2017; Eberhardt and Huckauf, 2020).
evidence: This describes the methods used in cited studies.

claim: Eberhardt and Huckauf, 2017 found that a small difference in depth (0.06 diopters) between the stimuli and fixation planes had no effect on the amount of crowding.
source: The authors found that this small difference in depth between the stimuli and fixation planes had no effect on the amount of crowding compared to when everything was presented at the fixation plane (Eberhardt and Huckauf, 2017).
evidence: This summarizes findings from a cited study.

claim: Eberhardt and Huckauf, 2019 found that crowding was greater when the stimuli were furthest from fixation compared to when they were closer to fixation, regardless of whether the stimuli were in front or behind the fixation plane.
source: The results showed that crowding was greater when the stimuli were furthest from fixation compared to when they were closer to fixation, regardless of whether the stimuli were in front or behind the fixation plane (Eberhardt and Huckauf, 2019).
evidence: This summarizes findings from a cited study.

claim: Eberhardt and Huckauf, 2020 found that when flanker depth was varied while the target was at fixation depth, crowding increased with increasing target-flanker depth difference.
source: When flanker depth was varied while the target was at fixation depth, crowding increased with increasing target-flanker depth difference (Eberhardt and Huckauf, 2020).
evidence: This summarizes findings from a cited study.

claim: The finding of Eberhardt and Huckauf, 2020 that crowding increased with target-flanker depth difference is the opposite to the findings of other studies using small stereoscopic disparities.
source: This result is the opposite to the findings of other studies in which small differences in depth between the target and flankers were introduced with stereoscopic disparity (Astle et al., 2014; Felisberti et al., 2005; Kooi et al., 1994; Sayim et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a comparison between findings from different studies.

claim: Eberhardt and Huckauf, 2020 found that when flanker depth was varied while the target was at fixation depth, crowding was greater when the flankers were behind the target and fixation compared to in front of it.
source: Furthermore, the authors also found that when flanker depth was varied while the target was at fixation depth, crowding was greater when the flankers were behind the target and fixation compared to in front of it (Eberhardt and Huckauf, 2020).
evidence: This summarizes findings from a cited study.

claim: Eberhardt and Huckauf, 2020 found that when target depth was varied while the flankers were at fixation, there was more crowding when the target was in front of the flankers and fixation compared to when it was behind them.
source: When target depth was varied while the flankers were at fixation, there was more crowding when the target was in front of the flankers and fixation compared to when it was behind them (Eberhardt and Huckauf, 2020).
evidence: This summarizes findings from a cited study.

claim: The multi-depth plane display consisted of screens at 0.4 m (near screen), 1.26 m (mid screen), and 4 m (far screen) viewing distances.
source: Therefore, using a novel multi-depth plane display consisting of screens at 0.4 m (near screen), 1.26 m (mid screen), and 4 m (far screen) viewing distances (Figure 2), we investigate how crowding is affected by large, real differences in target-flanker depth.
evidence: This describes the experimental apparatus used in the study, with reference to Figure 2.

claim: The viewing distances of 4 m, 1.26 m, and 0.4 m were chosen because 4 m is close to optical infinity while 0.4 m is the clinical standard for near distance, with 1.26 m being in the middle of these two extremes in log units.
source: These viewing distances were chosen because 4 m is close to optical infinity while 0.4 m is the clinical standard for near distance, with 1.26 m being in the middle of these two extremes in log units.
evidence: This explains the rationale for the experimental design choices.

claim: The near, mid, and far screens were at 2.5 diopters, 0.79 diopters and 0.25 diopters respectively.
source: Given in diopters, the near, mid, and far screens were at 2.5 diopters, 0.79 diopters and 0.25 diopters receptively.
evidence: This provides the optical specifications of the experimental setup.

claim: In Experiment 1, perceptual error was higher when the flanker ring was displayed in front of, or behind, the target and fixation plane.
source: Perceptual error was higher when the flanker ring was displayed in front of, or behind, the target and fixation plane (mixed effects multiple linear regression models compared via LRT for effect of flanker depth: χ2(2)=20.67, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claim: In Experiment 1, perceptual error decreased as target-flanker spacing increased.
source: As expected, perceptual error decreased as target-flanker spacing increased (effect of target-flanker spacing: χ2(1)=31.71, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claim: In Experiment 1, there was no significant interaction between flanker depth and target-flanker spacing.
source: There was no significant interaction between flanker depth and target-flanker spacing (χ2(2)=5.56, p=0.062).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 2, perceptual error tended to increase with increasing flanker depth when the flanker ring was behind the target and fixation plane.
source: Perceptual error tended to increase with increasing flanker depth when the flanker ring was behind the target and fixation plane, however, the effect of flanker depth was much weaker when the flanker ring was in front of the target and fixation (interaction between target-fixation depth and flanker depth: χ2(2)=17.18, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claim: In Experiment 2, the effect of flanker depth was much weaker when the flanker ring was in front of the target and fixation.
source: Perceptual error tended to increase with increasing flanker depth when the flanker ring was behind the target and fixation plane, however, the effect of flanker depth was much weaker when the flanker ring was in front of the target and fixation (interaction between target-fixation depth and flanker depth: χ2(2)=17.18, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claim: In Experiment 2, perceptual error decreased with increasing target-flanker spacing, in a manner corresponding to target-fixation depth.
source: Perceptual error decreased with increasing target-flanker spacing, in a manner corresponding to target-fixation depth (interaction between target-flanker spacing and target-fixation depth: χ2(1)=9.2, p=0.002).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claim: In Experiment 3, overall perceptual error was higher when the target was displayed in front of, or behind, the flanker ring and fixation.
source: Overall, perceptual error was higher when the target was displayed in front of, or behind, the flanker ring and fixation (effect of target depth: χ2(2)=36.93, p<0.001), with the greatest perceptual error occurring when the target was behind the flanker ring and fixation.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claim: In Experiment 3, the greatest perceptual error occurred when the target was behind the flanker ring and fixation.
source: Overall, perceptual error was higher when the target was displayed in front of, or behind, the flanker ring and fixation (effect of target depth: χ2(2)=36.93, p<0.001), with the greatest perceptual error occurring when the target was behind the flanker ring and fixation.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claim: In Experiment 3, perceptual error decreased as target-flanker spacing increased.
source: Perceptual error decreased as target-flanker spacing increased (effect of target-flanker spacing: χ2(1)=45.99, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claim: In Experiment 4, perceptual error was greatest when the target was displayed behind the flanker ring and fixation.
source: Perceptual error was greatest when the target was displayed behind the flanker ring and fixation, while the effect of depth was less prominent when the target was displayed in front of the flanker ring and fixation (interaction between flanker-fixation depth and target depth: χ2(2)=61.87, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claim: In Experiment 4, the effect of depth was less prominent when the target was displayed in front of the flanker ring and fixation.
source: Perceptual error was greatest when the target was displayed behind the flanker ring and fixation, while the effect of depth was less prominent when the target was displayed in front of the flanker ring and fixation (interaction between flanker-fixation depth and target depth: χ2(2)=61.87, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claim: In Experiment 4, perceptual error decreased as target-flanker spacing increased.
source: Perceptual error decreased as target-flanker spacing increased (effect of target-flanker spacing: χ2(1)=29.92, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claim: In Experiment 5, perceptual error decreased as target-flanker spacing increased.
source: Perceptual error decreased as target-flanker spacing increased (effect of target-flanker spacing: χ2(1)=64.8, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claim: In Experiment 5, there was a significant effect of target-flanker-fixation depth resulting from a higher perceptual error for stimuli displayed at 4 m.
source: There was also a significant effect of target-flanker-fixation depth (χ2(2)=8.75, p=0.013) resulting from a higher perceptual error for stimuli displayed at 4 m.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claim: In Experiment 1, when the flanker ring was away from target-fixation depth there was a reduction in the proportion of observers who consistently reported seeing the target within the flanker ring when the target-flanker spacing was small.
source: However, when the flanker ring was away from target-fixation depth there was a reduction in the proportion of observers who consistently reported seeing the target within the flanker ring when the target-flanker spacing was small (mixed effects binary logistic regression models compared via LRT; interaction between target-flanker spacing and flanker depth: χ2(2)=36.12, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claim: In Experiment 1, the effect of reduced proportion of observers reporting the target within the flanker ring was greatest when the flanker ring was displayed behind the target and fixation.
source: This effect was greatest when the flanker ring was displayed behind the target and fixation.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 2, when the flanker ring was away from target-fixation depth, there was a reduction in the overall proportion of trials in which observers reported seeing the target within the flanker ring.
source: As with the previous experiment, when the flanker ring was away from target-fixation depth, there was a reduction in the overall proportion of trials in which observers reported seeing the target within the flanker ring (interaction between target-fixation depth and flanker depth: χ2(2)=374.26, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claim: In Experiment 2, the greatest reduction in proportion of trials with target reported inside flanker ring occurred when target-flanker spacing was smaller.
source: The greatest reduction occurred when target-flanker spacing was smaller (effect of target-flanker spacing: χ2(1)=178.65, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claim: In Experiment 3, when the target was away from flanker-fixation depth, observers were less likely to report seeing the target within the flanker ring.
source: When the target was away from flanker-fixation depth, observers were less likely to report seeing the target within the flanker ring. This effect was greatest when target-flanker spacing was smaller and when the target was displayed in front of the flanker ring and fixation (interaction between target-flanker spacing and target depth: χ2(2)=100.38, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claim: In Experiment 3, the effect of reduced likelihood of reporting target within flanker ring was greatest when target-flanker spacing was smaller and when the target was displayed in front of the flanker ring and fixation.
source: When the target was away from flanker-fixation depth, observers were less likely to report seeing the target within the flanker ring. This effect was greatest when target-flanker spacing was smaller and when the target was displayed in front of the flanker ring and fixation (interaction between target-flanker spacing and target depth: χ2(2)=100.38, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claim: In Experiment 4, the greater the difference between target depth and flanker-fixation depth, the less likely observers were to report seeing the target within the flanker ring.
source: As with the previous experiment, the greater the difference between target depth and flanker-fixation depth, the less likely observers were to report seeing the target within the flanker ring (interaction between flanker-fixation depth and target depth: χ2(2)=779.49, p<0.001), particularly when target-flanker spacing was small (interaction between target-flanker spacing and target depth: χ2(2)=23.27, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claim: In Experiment 4, target-flanker spacing had a weaker effect on the proportion of trials in which observers reported seeing the target within the flanker ring when the flanker ring and fixation were near compared to far.
source: However, target-flanker spacing had a weaker effect on the proportion of trials in which observers reported seeing the target within the flanker ring when the flanker ring and fixation were near compared to far (interaction between target-flanker spacing and flanker-fixation depth: χ2(1)=56.23, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claim: The overall effects reported in the main study are also apparent in most of the experienced observers.
source: Nevertheless, the overall effects reported above are also apparent in most of the experienced observers (Figure 10).
evidence: This is a finding from the experienced observer data with reference to Figure 10.

claim: Even among highly trained, experienced observers there is a large amount of variation both between and within subjects.
source: However, Figure 10 shows that even among highly trained, experienced observers there is a large amount of variation both between and within subjects.
evidence: This is an observation from the experienced observer data with reference to Figure 10.

claim: The variation in perceptual error between subjects cannot solely be explained by differences in the perceived position of the target relative to the flanker ring.
source: The variation in perceptual error between subjects cannot solely be explained by differences in the perceived position of the target relative to the flanker ring (Figure 10—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is an inference from the data comparing perceptual error and perceived target position.

claim: In all experiments, perceptual error generally decreased as the target-flanker spacing increased, which is in line with previous crowding research.
source: In all experiments, perceptual error generally decreased as the target-flanker spacing increased, which is in line with previous crowding research (Bouma, 1970; Pelli, 2008).
evidence: This summarizes a consistent finding across experiments and relates it to previous research.

claim: Overall, perceptual error was higher when the target or flanker ring were presented at a different depth from the other and from fixation.
source: Overall, perceptual error was higher when the target or flanker ring were presented at a different depth from the other and from fixation.
evidence: This is a summary of findings across experiments.

claim: The greatest differences in perceptual error among the different depth conditions occurred when the target or flanker ring were presented behind fixation depth.
source: The greatest differences in perceptual error among the different depth conditions occurred when the target or flanker ring were presented behind fixation depth.
evidence: This is a summary of findings across experiments.

claim: When the target or flanker ring were presented in front of fixation depth, the differences in perceptual error among depth conditions were notably smaller.
source: In contrast, when the target or flanker ring were presented in front of fixation depth, the differences in perceptual error among depth conditions were notably smaller.
evidence: This is a summary of findings across experiments.

claim: When the target, flanker ring and fixation were all at the same depth plane, crowding tended to increase with the absolute distance of the stimuli from the observer.
source: The results also show that when the target, flanker ring and fixation were all at the same depth plane, crowding tended to increase with the absolute distance of the stimuli from the observer.
evidence: This is a finding from Experiment 5.

claim: In all the main experiments with naive observers there was a large amount of variation within the data.
source: However, in all the main experiments with naive observers there was a large amount of variation within the data.
evidence: This is an observation about the data quality and variability.

claim: Follow up experiments with experienced observers were largely consistent with the main effects observed in the main study.
source: Follow up experiments with a small sample of highly trained, experienced observers were largely consistent with the main effects observed in the main study.
evidence: This compares findings between naive and experienced observer groups.

claim: The experienced observers exhibited a high degree of between subject variation.
source: Moreover, the experienced observers also exhibited a high degree of between subject variation, which supports the suggestion that the variability in the main data from the large sample of naive observers is representative of the natural variation between different individuals.
evidence: This is an observation from the experienced observer data.

claim: Although significant effects were found at the population level, the effects of large differences in target-flanker depth can be highly variable at the individual level.
source: Therefore, although significant effects were found at the population level, the effects of large differences in target-flanker depth can be highly variable at the individual level.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing population-level and individual-level data.

claim: The main finding that a depth difference between the flankers and the target led to an increase in perceptual error is different from the findings of several previous studies using stereoscopic presentation.
source: The main finding that a depth difference between the flankers and the target led to an increase, rather than a decrease, in perceptual error is different from the findings of several previous studies that investigated the effect of depth on crowding using a stereoscopic presentation (Astle et al., 2014; Felisberti et al., 2005; Kooi et al., 1994; Sayim et al., 2008).
evidence: This compares the current findings with previous research.

claim: Several explanations for crowding have been proposed in which crowding occurs because target and flanking features are inappropriately grouped.
source: Several explanations for crowding have been proposed in which crowding occurs because target and flanking features are inappropriately grouped (Banks et al., 1979; Herzog and Manassi, 2015; Pachai et al., 2016).
evidence: This summarizes theoretical explanations from the literature.

claim: Crowding can be alleviated when the flankers are grouped together and segmented from the target.
source: Consistent with this explanation, crowding can be alleviated when the flankers are grouped together and segmented from the target (Herzog and Manassi, 2015).
evidence: This summarizes findings from the literature.

claim: The current results challenge the view that crowding occurs because target and flanking features are inappropriately grouped.
source: Our results challenge this view of crowding because it would predict that increasing the depth difference between target and flankers would decrease the probability of them being inappropriately grouped and increase the probability of the flankers being segmented from the target, thereby decreasing perceptual error, the opposite of our finding.
evidence: This is an inference from the current findings in relation to existing theory.

claim: Other models of crowding such as texture processing, feature integration, sampling errors, attentional resolution limits, or saccade properties are agnostic concerning the influence of depth differences among targets and flankers.
source: Other models of crowding, such as texture processing and feature integration (Balas et al., 2009; Freeman and Simoncelli, 2011; Parkes et al., 2001; van den Berg et al., 2012; Wallis and Bex, 2012), sampling errors (Ester et al., 2015; Ester et al., 2014; Harrison and Bex, 2017; Harrison and Bex, 2016; Harrison and Bex, 2015), attentional resolution limits (He et al., 1996) or saccade properties (Nandy and Tjan, 2012) are agnostic concerning the influence of depth differences among targets and flankers.
evidence: This is an evaluation of existing theoretical models in relation to depth effects.

claim: Each of the agnostic crowding models would require modification to explain the increase in crowding observed with large real depth differences between a target and its flankers.
source: Therefore, each of these models would require modification to explain the increase in crowding that we observe with large real depth differences between a target and its flankers.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of the current findings for existing theory.

claim: The current results agree with the findings of Eberhardt and Huckauf, 2020 who also used a real-depth display.
source: In contrast with studies that controlled depth with small stereoscopic disparities, our results do agree with the findings of Eberhardt and Huckauf, 2020 who also used a real-depth display and tested larger differences in depth between the target and flankers than previous studies had examined, though depth differences were still much smaller than those tested in our current study.
evidence: This compares the current findings with a specific previous study.

claim: The current findings from Experiments 1 and 2 are consistent with Eberhardt and Huckauf, 2020's results showing increased crowding with target-flanker depth difference and greater crowding when flankers were behind versus in front of the target.
source: When the target was at fixation depth (comparable to Experiments 1 and 2 in our study), Eberhardt and Huckauf, 2020 found that crowding increased with increasing target-flanker depth difference. The authors also found that crowding was greater when the flankers were behind the target and fixation compared to in front of it (Eberhardt and Huckauf, 2020). Our findings from Experiments 1 and 2 are consistent with these results.
evidence: This compares the current findings with a specific previous study.

claim: In Experiments 3 and 4, perceptual error was greatest when the target was presented behind the flanker ring and fixation rather than in front of it, which differs from Eberhardt and Huckauf, 2020.
source: However, when the flankers were at fixation depth (comparable to Experiments 3 and 4 in our study), Eberhardt and Huckauf, 2020 found that crowding was higher when the target was in front of the flankers and fixation compared to when it was behind them. In contrast, in Experiments 3 and 4 we found that perceptual error was greatest when the target was presented behind the flanker ring and fixation rather than in front of it.
evidence: This compares the current findings with a specific previous study and notes a difference.

claim: The difference between the current study and Eberhardt and Huckauf, 2020 is likely due to a combination of high defocus blur when the target was behind fixation combined with the finding that larger absolute distance from the observer resulted in higher perceptual error.
source: This difference is likely due to a combination of high defocus blur when the target was behind fixation combined with the finding from Experiment 5 which found that in our study a larger absolute distance from the observer resulted in higher perceptual error.
evidence: This is an inference explaining the difference between studies.

claim: The current results, together with those from previous studies, suggest that small differences in depth between the target and flankers reduce crowding while larger differences in depth can increase it.
source: Our results, together with those from previous studies, suggest that small differences in depth between the target and flankers reduce crowding (Astle et al., 2014; Felisberti et al., 2005; Kooi et al., 1994; Sayim et al., 2008), while larger differences in depth can increase it (Eberhardt and Huckauf, 2020 and results from our study).
evidence: This is a synthesis of findings from the current study and previous research.

claim: There is precedent for non-linear effects of depth on perceptual processing outside the crowding literature.
source: Although this pattern is quite surprising, there is precedent for non-linear effects of depth on perceptual processing outside the crowding literature.
evidence: This contextualizes the findings within broader perceptual research.

claim: In a multiple object tracking task, when targets and distractors were distributed equally on two depth planes, tracking accuracy was better than on a single depth plane when the depth difference was small (~6 cm) but worse when the depth difference was large (50 cm).
source: In a multiple object tracking task, when the targets and distractors were distributed equally on two depth planes, tracking accuracy was better than the accuracy during trials in which targets and distractors appeared on a single depth plane when the depth difference between planes was small (~6 cm) (Ur Rehman et al., 2015; Viswanathan and Mingolla, 2002), but worse when the depth difference between planes was large (50 cm) (Ur Rehman et al., 2015).
evidence: This summarizes findings from previous research on depth effects in a different task.

claim: The geometry of the eyes and the 3D environment create interocular disparity differences between the images in each eye.
source: The geometry of the eyes and the 3D environment create interocular disparity differences between the images in each eye.
evidence: This is established knowledge about binocular vision.

claim: When corresponding features in the images in each eye can be identified, the images can be fused to generate a binocular perceptual experience of depth.
source: When corresponding features in the images in each eye can be identified, the images can be fused to generate a binocular perceptual experience of depth (for review see Nityananda and Read, 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about binocular vision supported by a review citation.

claim: There is a horizontal and vertical spatial limit to the interocular disparity difference over which the visual system attempts to identify corresponding retinal points in order to fuse different 2D interocular images as a single 3D object.
source: There is a horizontal and vertical spatial limit to the interocular disparity difference over which the visual system attempts to identify corresponding retinal points in order to fuse different 2D interocular images as a single 3D object (Westheimer, 1979).
evidence: This is established knowledge about binocular vision supported by citation.

claim: This 2D spatial correspondence limit creates a 3D volume along the horopter known as Panum's Fusional Area.
source: This 2D spatial correspondence limit creates a 3D volume along the horopter known as Panum's Fusional Area (Panum, 1858).
evidence: This is established knowledge about binocular vision supported by citation.

claim: Outside Panum's Fusional Area, there is a loss of stereoscopic depth perception and either double vision (diplopia) may be experienced, or single vision may occur if the image from one eye is partly suppressed.
source: Outside Panum's Fusional Area, there is a loss of stereoscopic depth perception and either double vision (diplopia) may be experienced, or single vision may occur if the image from one eye is partly suppressed (Georgeson and Wallis, 2014; Ono et al., 1977; Spiegel et al., 2016; Stidwill and Fletcher, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about binocular vision supported by citations.

claim: The spatial extent of Panum's Fusional Area depends on the spatial frequency of the stimuli.
source: The spatial extent of Panum's Fusional Area depends on the spatial frequency of the stimuli (Maiello et al., 2020; Pulliam, 1981; Reynaud and Hess, 2017; Wilcox and Allison, 2009; Yang and Blake, 1991) and increases with eccentricity (Hampton and Kertesz, 1983; Harrold and Grove, 2019; Qin et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge about binocular vision supported by citations.

claim: The spatial extent of Panum's Fusional Area increases with eccentricity.
source: The spatial extent of Panum's Fusional Area depends on the spatial frequency of the stimuli (Maiello et al., 2020; Pulliam, 1981; Reynaud and Hess, 2017; Wilcox and Allison, 2009; Yang and Blake, 1991) and increases with eccentricity (Hampton and Kertesz, 1983; Harrold and Grove, 2019; Qin et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge about binocular vision supported by citations.

claim: It is possible that differences between fusion and depth perception within Panum's Fusional Area versus diplopia and/or local suppression outside of it can explain the patterns of results observed between studies.
source: It is possible that differences between fusion and depth perception within Panum's Fusional Area versus diplopia, and/or local suppression for single vision, outside of it can explain the patterns of results observed between studies.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the findings.

claim: Small disparity differences between target and flankers create differences in perceived depth that can alleviate the effects of crowding, potentially through ungrouping of target and flanking elements or by independent processing in different depth-selective channels.
source: Small disparity differences between target and flankers create differences in perceived depth that can alleviate the effects of crowding, potentially through ungrouping of target and flanking elements (Herzog et al., 2015; Herzog and Manassi, 2015; Manassi et al., 2012) or by independent processing of target and flankers in different depth-selective channels (Norcia et al., 1985; Pulliam, 1981; Reynaud and Hess, 2017; Tyler et al., 1994; Wilcox and Allison, 2009; Yang and Blake, 1991) by any of the computational models of crowding based on texture processing and feature integration (Balas et al., 2009; Freeman and Simoncelli, 2011; Parkes et al., 2001; van den Berg et al., 2012; Wallis and Bex, 2012), sampling errors (Ester et al., 2015; Ester et al., 2014; Harrison and Bex, 2017; Harrison and Bex, 2016; Harrison and Bex, 2015) attentional resolution limits (He et al., 1996) or saccade properties (Nandy and Tjan, 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citations to relevant theories and findings.

claim: Large interocular disparity differences can induce diplopia that could increase the perceived number of flankers.
source: Large interocular disparity differences on the other hand can induce diplopia that could increase the perceived number of flankers (Eberhardt and Huckauf, 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citation.

claim: A perceived increase in the number of flanking elements could result in higher perceptual error because increasing the number of flankers is known to increase crowding under certain conditions.
source: In theory, this perceived increase in the number of flanking elements could result in higher perceptual error because increasing the number of flankers is known to increase crowding under certain conditions (Chanceaux et al., 2014; Manassi et al., 2012; Pluháček et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citations.

claim: Reduced crowding with increasing number of flankers can occur in cases where the additional flankers are grouped together.
source: It is however worth noting that the opposite can occur, that is reduced crowding with increasing number of flankers, in cases where the additional flankers are grouped together (Manassi et al., 2013; Manassi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a qualification of the previous claim supported by citations.

claim: When asked, only a few of the naive observers reported experiencing diplopia.
source: Surprisingly, when asked, only a few of the naive observers reported experiencing diplopia, and those that did reported only experiencing it in a minority of presentations for which they selected the 'unsure or no ring' option (see Methods) when reporting the perceived location of the target (Figure 8—figure supplements 1E and 2E, and Figure 9—figure supplements 1E and 2E).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Among the four experienced observers, three verbally reported experiencing diplopia during some of the conditions.
source: However, among the four experienced observers, three verbally reported experiencing diplopia during some of the conditions for which they either selected the 'unsure or no ring' option (Figure 10—figure supplement 2E and Figure 11—figure supplement 2E), or in cases when the diplopia was barely visible, they chose the option that was the closest match to the clearest stimulus image.
evidence: This is an observation from the experienced observer data.

claim: The fact that the experienced observers were more likely to report experiencing diplopia raises the possibility that diplopia may have been more common among the naive observers than was indicated by asking them.
source: The fact that the experienced observers were more likely to report experiencing diplopia, possibly because they were better at recognizing it, raises the possibility that diplopia may have been more common among the naive observers than was indicated by asking them.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing naive and experienced observer reports.

claim: One of the four experienced observers reported that they never experienced diplopia in any of the experiments.
source: However, it is worth noting that one of the four experienced observers reported that they never experienced diplopia in any of the experiments, which is more consistent with the majority of naive observers.
evidence: This is an observation from the experienced observer data.

claim: It is possible that the short presentation time of the stimulus was too fast for most observers to notice diplopia consciously.
source: It is possible that the short presentation time of the stimulus was too fast for most observers to notice diplopia consciously (i.e. diplopia did not enter awareness), or that diplopia was suppressed entirely by local suppression to maintain single vision.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the low reports of diplopia.

claim: Attention effects such as inattentional blindness could play a role in explaining why so few observers reported diplopia.
source: Attention effects such as inattentional blindness (Bredemeier and Simons, 2012; Simons and Chabris, 1999) could also play a role in explaining why so few observers reported diplopia in the main experiments.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citations.

claim: There is conflicting evidence as to whether conscious awareness of a flanker is necessary for it to induce crowding.
source: There is conflicting evidence as to whether conscious awareness of a flanker is necessary for it to induce crowding (compare Ho and Cheung, 2011 vs Wallis and Bex, 2011), and thus whether 'unconscious diplopia' could have increased crowding in this study due to the reason highlighted above is a matter for debate and beyond the scope of our findings.
evidence: This acknowledges conflicting evidence in the literature.

claim: Due to the lack of binocular fusion of stimulus areas outside Panum's Fusional Area, the possible involvement of binocular rivalry cannot be ruled out.
source: In addition, it is worth noting that due to the lack of binocular fusion of stimulus areas outside Panum's Fusional Area, we can't rule out the possible involvement of binocular rivalry which has been shown to interfere with object recognition not just in isolation but also when combined with crowding (Kim et al., 2013).
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation and alternative explanation supported by citation.

claim: Another explanation for higher perceptual error with increasing target-flanker depth differences could be perceived target misalignment.
source: Another explanation for higher perceptual error with increasing target-flanker depth differences could be perceived target misalignment.
evidence: This proposes an alternative explanation for the findings.

claim: At the start of Experiments 1–4 each observer performed a subjective spatial calibration to ensure that the angular positions of the stimuli and fixation point relative to primary gaze were consistent across all three depth planes.
source: As explained in the Methods, at the start of Experiments 1–4 each observer performed a subjective spatial calibration to ensure that the angular positions of the stimuli and fixation point relative to primary gaze were consistent across all three depth planes.
evidence: This describes a methodological procedure.

claim: The spatial calibration had to be performed monocularly using the observer's dominant eye to avoid confusion caused by diplopia or rivalry.
source: Although the main experiments were performed under binocular viewing conditions, this spatial calibration had to be performed monocularly using the observer's dominant eye to avoid confusion caused by diplopia or rivalry (see Methods).
evidence: This explains a methodological decision.

claim: The screens were imperfectly aligned for the non-dominant eye.
source: This means that the screens were imperfectly aligned for the non-dominant eye.
evidence: This is an inference from the monocular calibration procedure.

claim: At certain flanker sizes and separations there may be occlusions between target and flanker features that could affect target report accuracy, which is not the same mechanism as crowding.
source: Therefore, as in the real world, at certain flanker sizes and separations there may be occlusions between target and flanker features that could affect target report accuracy, which is not the same mechanism as crowding.
evidence: This is an inference about potential confounds in the data.

claim: When perceptual error was recalculated using only trials in which the observer reported seeing the target inside the flanker ring, the effect of flanker and/or target depth remained statistically significant in all experiments except Experiment 2.
source: To examine how target misalignment affected the overall results, we recalculated perceptual error for the main experiments with naive observers using only trials in which the observer reported seeing the target inside the flanker ring. We then reanalyzed these data the same way as for perceptual error calculated from the full data set (see Methods). Apart from Experiment 2, the effect of flanker and/or target depth remained statistically significant (see Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1 for plots and analysis results).
evidence: This is a finding from a supplementary analysis.

claim: Across the majority of experiments, misalignment or occlusion of the target by the flanker ring is not enough to explain the overall results.
source: Therefore, across the majority of experiments, misalignment or occlusion of the target by the flanker ring is not enough to explain the overall results.
evidence: This is an inference from the supplementary analysis.

claim: The increase in perceptual error when the target and flankers are at different depths is being driven by an increase in crowding.
source: This supports the suggestion that the increase in perceptual error when the target and flankers are at different depths is being driven by an increase in crowding.
evidence: This is an inference from the supplementary analysis.

claim: This current study is the first to investigate how crowding is affected by large, real differences in depth between a target and flanking features.
source: This current study is the first to investigate how crowding is affected by large, real differences in depth between a target and flanking features.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study.

claim: Objects in the real world are often flanked by visual features that vary greatly in their distance from an observer, and many will fall outside the limits of Panum's Fusional Area.
source: This is important because objects in the real world are often flanked by visual features that vary greatly in their distance from an observer, and many will fall outside the limits of Panum's Fusional Area (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a statement about real-world conditions with reference to Figure 1.

claim: A limitation of the current approach is that the use of relatively simple stimuli in a tightly controlled experiment limits the generalizability of the findings to the real world where clutter is abundant and more complex.
source: A limitation of our approach is that the use of relatively simple stimuli in a tightly controlled experiment limits the generalizability of our findings to the real world where clutter is abundant and more complex.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the study.

claim: Future research should aim to utilize stimuli that better capture the complexity and heterogeneity of natural scenes.
source: Future research should therefore aim to utilize stimuli that better capture the complexity and heterogeneity of natural scenes.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research.

claim: Future work should investigate if the reported effects of depth on crowding hold at different target eccentricities.
source: Future work should also investigate if the reported effects of depth on crowding in our study hold at different target eccentricities, particularly given that the range of Panum's Fusional Area changes with eccentricity (Hampton and Kertesz, 1983; Harrold and Grove, 2019; Qin et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research supported by citations.

claim: The findings show that crowding from clutter outside Panum's Fusional Area has the potential to significantly impact object recognition and visual perception in the peripheral field.
source: Nevertheless, our findings still show that crowding from clutter outside Panum's Fusional Area has the potential to significantly impact object recognition and visual perception in the peripheral field.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the findings.

claim: The findings do not support the view that depth differences between targets and flankers necessarily reduce crowding.
source: Our findings therefore do not support the view that depth differences between targets and flankers necessarily reduce crowding, instead the effect of depth on crowding appears to be more complex than originally thought.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the findings.

claim: The effect of depth on crowding appears to be more complex than originally thought.
source: Our findings therefore do not support the view that depth differences between targets and flankers necessarily reduce crowding, instead the effect of depth on crowding appears to be more complex than originally thought.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the findings.

claim: Data collected from experienced participants shows that the overall trends at the population level may not always be apparent at the individual level.
source: Furthermore, data collected from experienced participants shows that the overall trends at the population level may not always be apparent at the individual level.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing population and individual data.

claim: The results suggest that small differences in depth between targets and flankers do not have the same effect on crowding as larger differences in depth in which either the target or flankers are presented outside the limits of binocular fusion.
source: Nonetheless, our results, alongside those of previous studies, suggest that small differences in depth between targets and flankers do not have the same effect on crowding as larger differences in depth in which either the target or flankers are presented outside the limits of binocular fusion.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the current findings with previous research.

claim: This finding confirms the potential importance and relevance of crowding in three-dimensional scenes.
source: This finding confirms the potential importance and relevance of crowding in three-dimensional scenes.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: A total of 110 naive subjects were recruited from the Northeastern University undergraduate population.
source: For the main study, a total of 110 naive subjects were recruited from the Northeastern University undergraduate population in exchange for course credit as compensation for their time.
evidence: This describes the participant recruitment for the study.

claim: Seven subjects were excluded immediately following screening because they did not meet the inclusion criteria of normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
source: Of these, seven were excluded immediately following screening because they did not meet the inclusion criteria of normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
evidence: This describes participant exclusion criteria.

claim: An additional five subjects were excluded because of issues with the experimental code, calibration issues, or because they did not follow the task instructions.
source: An additional five subjects were excluded because of issues with the experimental code (N=3), calibration issues (N=1) or because they did not follow the task instructions (N=1).
evidence: This describes participant exclusion criteria.

claim: A total of 98 subjects contributed usable data across five separate experiments.
source: Thus, a total of 98 subjects (32 males, 66 females; mean age = 18.86 years) contributed usable data across five separate experiments (22 in Experiment 1, 19 in Experiment 2, 21 in Experiments 3 and 4, and 15 in Experiment 5).
evidence: This describes the final sample size and demographics.

claim: Four 'experienced subjects' participated in all five experiments in a random order.
source: In addition to the naive subjects who each participated in one of the five experiments as part of the main study, we also separately tested four 'experienced subjects' (2 males, 2 females; mean age = 29 years) who participated in all five experiments in a random order.
evidence: This describes the experienced observer sample.

claim: All the experienced subjects were volunteers from within the university vision research community and were extremely familiar and well-practiced in participating in psychophysics experiments.
source: All the experienced subjects (none of whom were the authors) were volunteers from within the university vision research community and were therefore extremely familiar and well-practiced in participating in psychophysics experiments such as those in our current study.
evidence: This describes the characteristics of the experienced observer sample.

claim: The purpose of repeating the study with experienced subjects was to enable better exploration of the effects of depth at the individual level.
source: The purpose of repeating the study with a small group of highly trained, experienced subjects who participated in all five experiments was to enable us to better explore the effects of depth at the individual level.
evidence: This explains the rationale for including experienced observers.

claim: The experimental procedure was approved by the institutional review board at Northeastern University.
source: The experimental procedure was approved by the institutional review board at Northeastern University, and the experiments were performed in accordance with the tenets of the Declaration of Helsinki.
evidence: This describes ethical approval for the study.

claim: The design of the multi-depth plane display enables observers to simultaneously view adjacent stimuli presented on all three depth planes at the same time.
source: This design enables observers to simultaneously view adjacent stimuli presented on all three depth planes at the same time.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the experimental apparatus.

claim: The screens were temporally synchronized and spatially aligned to ensure display timing and position were consistent across the three depth planes.
source: The screens were temporally synchronized and spatially aligned (see Methods) to ensure display timing and position were consistent across the three depth planes.
evidence: This describes calibration procedures for the experimental apparatus.

claim: The target was a white Landolt-C displayed against a black background at 10° eccentricity to the right or left of the fixation point.
source: The target was a white Landolt-C displayed against a black background at 10° eccentricity to the right or left of the fixation point at primary gaze.
evidence: This describes the stimulus characteristics.

claim: The target was 1° in diameter with a 0.25° line width and a 0.25° opening.
source: Following the structure of a Landolt-C optotype, the target was 1° in diameter with a 0.25° line width and a 0.25° opening.
evidence: This describes the stimulus characteristics.

claim: The opening orientation of the target was random each trial, drawn from a uniform 360° distribution.
source: The opening orientation of the target was random each trial, drawn from a uniform 360° distribution.
evidence: This describes the stimulus randomization procedure.

claim: The target was surrounded by a white flanker ring formed of four circular arcs.
source: The target was surrounded by a white flanker ring formed of four circular arcs (Figure 3).
evidence: This describes the stimulus characteristics with reference to Figure 3.

claim: The outer edge of the target was separated from the inner edge of the flanker ring by 5°, 2.5°, 1.25° or 0.625°.
source: In each depth combination described below, the outer edge of the target was separated from the inner edge of the flanker ring by 5°, 2.5°, 1.25° or 0.625°.
evidence: This describes the stimulus spacing conditions.

claim: The target-flanker separations of 5°, 2.5°, 1.25°, and 0.625° represented 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, and 1/16 of the target eccentricity, respectively.
source: These distances of separation represented 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, and 1/16 of the target eccentricity, respectively.
evidence: This describes the rationale for the spacing conditions.

claim: For the experiments conducted with the four experienced subjects, the 5° target-flanker eccentricity condition was not included.
source: Note that for the experiments conducted with the four experienced subjects, the 5° target-flanker eccentricity condition was not included.
evidence: This describes a difference in the experimental design for experienced observers.

claim: The luminance of stimuli displayed on the near and far screens were calibrated to match the luminance of the mid screen.
source: Since the mid screen was dimmest (R=G=B=255, white = 13.56 cd/m2), the luminance of stimuli displayed on the near and far screens were calibrated to match the luminance of the mid screen using a Photo Research PR-650 spectroradiometer (Photo Research, Chatsworth, CA, USA).
evidence: This describes the luminance calibration procedure.

claim: The room lights were switched off for the duration of the experiment.
source: The room lights were switched off for the duration of the experiment.
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions.

claim: In Experiment 1, the target and fixation point were always on the mid screen while the flanker ring was displayed in front, behind or at fixation depth.
source: In Experiment 1, the target and fixation point were always on the mid screen while the flanker ring was displayed in front, behind or at fixation depth.
evidence: This describes the experimental design for Experiment 1.

claim: In Experiment 2, the target and fixation point were presented on the near or far screen while the depth of the flanker ring was varied.
source: In Experiment 2, the target and fixation point were presented on the near or far screen while the depth of the flanker ring was varied.
evidence: This describes the experimental design for Experiment 2.

claim: Experiments 3 and 4 were the same as Experiments 1 and 2 respectively except that the flanker ring was presented at fixation depth while the target depth was varied.
source: Experiments 3 and 4 were the same as Experiments 1 and 2 respectively except that the flanker ring was presented at fixation depth while the target depth was varied.
evidence: This describes the experimental design for Experiments 3 and 4.

claim: For Experiment 5, the target, flanker ring and fixation were presented together on the same screen at three different depths.
source: For Experiment 5, the target, flanker ring and fixation were presented together on the same screen at three different depths.
evidence: This describes the experimental design for Experiment 5.

claim: Experiment 5 was designed to investigate whether there was an effect of absolute viewing distance on crowding.
source: This was to investigate whether there was an effect of absolute viewing distance on crowding.
evidence: This explains the rationale for Experiment 5.

claim: Each condition was repeated 10 times in Experiments 1, 2, 3 and 5 and eight times in Experiment 4.
source: Each condition was repeated 10 times in Experiments 1, 2, 3 and 5 and eight times in Experiment 4, with equal number of repeats on either side of the fixation point.
evidence: This describes the number of repetitions per condition.

claim: The order of testing was randomized.
source: The order of testing was randomized.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: The target and flanker ring were displayed for 0.25 s.
source: The target and flanker ring (if present) were displayed for 0.25 s.
evidence: This describes the stimulus presentation duration.

claim: Observers used the mouse to rotate a Landolt-C until it matched the perceived orientation of the target and then clicked to report the orientation.
source: The observer used the mouse to rotate this Landolt-C until it matched the perceived orientation of the target and then clicked to report the orientation.
evidence: This describes the response method.

claim: In all experiments except Experiment 5, observers were asked to report the perceived location of the target relative to the position of the flanker ring.
source: In all experiments except Experiment 5, observers were also asked to report the perceived location of the target relative to the position of the flanker ring.
evidence: This describes an additional response measure.

claim: There were five options for reporting perceived target location: 'target in center of ring', 'target inside ring but not in the center', 'ring obstructs target', 'target outside ring', and 'unsure or no ring'.
source: There were five options to choose from, 'target in center of ring', 'target inside ring but not in the center', 'ring obstructs target', 'target outside ring', and 'unsure or no ring'.
evidence: This describes the response options.

claim: Perceptual error was calculated as the circular standard deviation of report errors for each stimulus condition.
source: To quantify crowding for each stimulus condition, we first calculated the report error for each presentation, that is, the angular difference between the reported gap orientation of the target and the actual gap orientation. For each subject, this generated 10 report errors per stimulus condition in Experiments 1, 2, 3, and 5, and eight per stimulus condition in Experiment 4. We then used these report errors to calculate the circular standard deviation for each stimulus condition using the Circular Statistics Toolbox (Berens, 2009) in MATLAB R2022a (MathWorks Inc, Natick, MA, USA). We refer to this measure as perceptual error, which is reported in degrees.
evidence: This describes the data analysis method.

claim: The effects of target/flanker depth and target-flanker spacing on perceptual error were analyzed using mixed effects multiple linear regression.
source: For the main study with naive observers, the effects of target/flanker depth and target-flanker spacing on perceptual error were analyzed using mixed effects multiple linear regression, fitted using the lme4 package (Bates et al., 2015) in R (R Development Core Team, 2022).
evidence: This describes the statistical analysis method.

claim: Perceptual error was natural log transformed to correct for positive skew.
source: Perceptual error was used as the response (dependent) variable after being natural log transformed to correct for positive skew.
evidence: This describes a data transformation procedure.

claim: Subject identification was included as a random effect in all experiments to control for repeated measures.
source: Subject identification (ID) was included as a random effect in all experiments to control for repeated measures.
evidence: This describes the statistical model structure.

claim: The control condition data were excluded to ensure that the fixed effects remained independent and the effect of having no flanker ring did not mask the effect of flanker and target depth.
source: This was to ensure that (a) the fixed effects remained independent and (b) the effect of having no flanker ring did not mask the effect of flanker and target depth.
evidence: This explains the rationale for excluding control condition data.
